lecture_context.lecture_title: What’s Going On Inside My Model?

unit.name: Modern transformer representation analysis
unit.description: Compares CNN visualization to transformer interpretation through attention, embeddings, and the current limits of transformer-circuits research.
unit.summary: The lecture transitions from CNNs to frontier models by saying CNNs visualize localized edges, textures, and shapes, while LLMs require visualizing relationships and meanings between tokens or concepts [ts=4388s] [ts=4400s]. Attention is framed as a transformer mechanism for relating a token to relevant surrounding tokens, with different heads potentially learning patterns such as pronoun-to-noun links or ordering constraints [ts=4469s] [ts=4494s]. Embeddings are introduced as the model’s internal map of meaning, where semantically similar tokens should lie close together and can be sanity-checked with dimensionality-reduction visualizations [ts=4551s] [ts=4596s]. The instructor cautions that modern transformers remain hard to interpret and points to transformer circuits and induction heads as frontier research rather than settled tooling [ts=4639s] [ts=4660s] [ts=4678s].

key_points.text: CNN interpretability focuses on localized visual features, whereas LLM interpretability focuses on relationships and meanings between tokens or concepts.
Attention maps visualize how a token relates to other tokens, functioning as a transformer analog to CNN saliency maps.
Different attention heads can learn different relational patterns, such as pronoun links, structure tracking, or ordering.
Embeddings encode tokens as vectors, and semantically similar tokens are expected to be nearby in embedding space.
Attention and embeddings together let language models track relationships and meanings.
Transformer circuits and induction heads are described as current research tools for interpreting transformer internals.
